title: Appeal votes at home and elsewhere
question: Does a supervisor vote to uphold appeals more often when the project is in their own district, and does the Board’s result match the district supervisor’s vote?
finding: On 142 decided appeals in a known district, the Board’s result matched the district supervisor’s vote 136 times (95.8%): 34 of the 37 they voted to uphold were upheld and 102 of the 105 they voted to reject were rejected. District supervisors voted to uphold at about the same rate (26.1%) as the other members on those same appeals (27.1% of 1,375 votes), and were excused or absent on 5 more.
how: For each appeal decided by a recorded vote, the deciding roll call is the passing vote on the adopted motion. A vote “to uphold” is an aye on a motion reversing or disapproving the decision appealed, or a no on a motion affirming it. “Own district” means the member held the seat of the district printed in the appeal’s title (or of the address). Per-member rates are printed only on 20 or more votes; members with fewer than 20 appeal votes in all are left out.
limits: Deciding votes on appeals are nearly always unanimous, so each member’s record mostly mirrors which appeals happened to be upheld while they sat. this table measures how closely the votes track it and cannot say why. The district supervisor made the deciding motion in 117 of these 142 appeals. Few members have 20 appeals in their own district. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
